--- title: "Data visualisation" execute: df-print: kable warning: false knitr: opts_chunk: fig.width: 5 fig.height: 4.2 --- In this episode, you will practice making honest, and beautiful, data visualisations using `ggplot2` in `RStudio`. You will start with the R Project you created in the previous episode. First, we will load the required package for this episode: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: We will work with the `palmerpenguins` dataset. This is a dataset describing 344 penguins. There are three different species, occuring on three different islands, and several parameters have been recorded. ::: {.column-margin} If you want to know more about this dataset, see [this nice slideshow](https://apreshill.github.io/palmerpenguins-useR-2022/#/what-is-palmerpenguins). ::: Let's have a look at the general properties of the dataset: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins <- read.csv('data/penguins.csv') head(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|species |island | bill_length_mm| bill_depth_mm| flipper_length_mm| body_mass_g|sex | year| |:-------|:---------|--------------:|-------------:|-----------------:|-----------:|:------|----:| |Adelie |Torgersen | 39.1| 18.7| 181| 3750|male | 2007| |Adelie |Torgersen | 39.5| 17.4| 186| 3800|female | 2007| |Adelie |Torgersen | 40.3| 18.0| 195| 3250|female | 2007| |Adelie |Torgersen | NA| NA| NA| NA|NA | 2007| |Adelie |Torgersen | 36.7| 19.3| 193| 3450|female | 2007| |Adelie |Torgersen | 39.3| 20.6| 190| 3650|male | 2007|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} str(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 344 obs. of 8 variables: $ species : chr "Adelie" "Adelie" "Adelie" "Adelie" ... $ island : chr "Torgersen" "Torgersen" "Torgersen" "Torgersen" ... $ bill_length_mm : num 39.1 39.5 40.3 NA 36.7 39.3 38.9 39.2 34.1 42 ... $ bill_depth_mm : num 18.7 17.4 18 NA 19.3 20.6 17.8 19.6 18.1 20.2 ... $ flipper_length_mm: int 181 186 195 NA 193 190 181 195 193 190 ... $ body_mass_g : int 3750 3800 3250 NA 3450 3650 3625 4675 3475 4250 ... $ sex : chr "male" "female" "female" NA ... $ year : int 2007 2007 2007 2007 2007 2007 2007 2007 2007 2007 ... ``` ::: ::: Indeed, the are 344 observations. We have some categorical data encoded as factors (`species`, `island`, `sex`) and some measurements of the bodies of the penguins (`bill_len`, `flipper_len`). To make a bar plot, we first need to calculate the mean and standard error. In this case, we will group by `species`, and calculate the mean `body_mass`: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_summary <- penguins %>% group_by(species) %>% summarize(mean = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), se = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n())) ``` ::: Let's inspect the results: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} head(penguins_summary) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|species | mean| se| |:---------|--------:|--------:| |Adelie | 3700.662| 37.19462| |Chinstrap | 3733.088| 46.60747| |Gentoo | 5076.016| 45.27097|
::: ::: Okay, looks like the Gentoo penguins have a much higher body mass than the other two species. ## From bar plot to sina plot Let's visualise the mean body mass using a 'traditional' barplot with error bars. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_summary %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = mean)) + geom_col() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: It does show what we just discovered, but it hides a lot. The standard error bars give some sort of idea of the spread of the data, but it looks suspicously small. That's because the standard error decreases with increasing sample size `n`, and in this case we have quite some penguins! What does the spread _really_ look like? A boxplot helps to solve this proble, at least partially: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Instead of the mean, boxplots highlight the _median_ value (thick line), the 25% and 75% percentile value (the box), and 1.5 * IQR (the lines) (where IQR is the inter-quartile range, or distance between the first and third quartiles). It's better, but it still hides the actual data. Let's add each individual datapoint. To do this, we use `geom_jitter()`. This function adds a little bit of noise on the x-axis direction. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: This is nice already! But we can let the shape that we're plotting _follow the distribution_ of the underlying datapoints rather than just plot boxes. The boxplots then become _violin_ plots: simply change `geom_boxplot()` for `geom_violin()` ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_violin() + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: This is an improvemen: we now see that the body weight distribution of Chinstrap penguins seems to be more narrow than the other two species. We can emphasize this more by letting the individual data points follow their distrution as well. To do that, we can change `geom_jitter` to `geom_quasirandom`, from the `ggbeeswarm` package. The combination of violin plot with individual datapoints that follow their distribution is called a _sina_ plot. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggbeeswarm) penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_violin() + geom_quasirandom(alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: This is starting to become an honest, information dense plot. However, the default choice of y-axis range exaggerates the difference in body mass between Gentoo penguins and the other species. We can update this by setting the `limits` of the `y` axis. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_violin() + geom_quasirandom(alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Let's think about Tufte's data visualisation principles for a moment. If we're really strict; we can say that for each species, the distribution of the data points is drawn twice. Once in the 'left' direction, and once in the 'right' direction. We can change this by moving from `geom_quasirandom()` to `geom_beeswarm()` with the `side = -1` argument ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_violin() + geom_beeswarm(side = -1, alpha = 0.5) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: We will now add just a bit more information to the plot: - We add the median value with a black line with the `geom_violin()` argument `draw_quantiles = 0.5` - We add the mean value with a blue dot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_violin(draw_quantiles = 0.5) + geom_beeswarm(side = -1, alpha = 0.5) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, colour = "steelblue", alpha = 1) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Nice! Also notice how we save the plot to a variable `p` this time. That way we can add styling options to the plot by _adding_ to the `p` variable. Let's now work a bit on the aestethics of the plot. To achieve a higher data-to-ink ratio, we remove the grey background and all grid lines. This is easy to do by just adding one of the default `themes` of R: ::: {.column-margin} If you want to easily style your plots like famous newspapers (like `wall street journal`), see [the ggthemes package](https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/). ::: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Okay, maybe this is a bit _too_ minimal for my taste; I want the major y-axis gridlines back. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_classic() + theme( panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey70") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Finally; let's update the axis labels: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} p2 <- p + theme_classic() + theme( panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey70")) + labs( x = "Penguin species", y = "Body mass (grams)") p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Finally, we can save the plot as `.png` (for presentations) and as `.pdf` (to make small adjustments to the plot in software like Illustrator or Inkscape, if necessary). ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave('results/body_mass_plot.png', p2, width = 5, height = 4, units = "in", create.dir = TRUE) ggsave('results/body_mass_plot.pdf', p2, width = 5, height = 4, units = "in", create.dir = TRUE) ``` ::: ## Creating small multiples Now, we will demonstrate the power of small multiples. Say we're interested in the relationshop between bill length and bill depth. We can visualize this with a scatter plot. We add a regression line via `geom_smooth()`. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = FALSE) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Okay, so, the bill depth seems to be negatively correlated to the bill length! Let's color the points by species, to inspect whether this correlation holds for all different species. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Woah! When looking per species; the negative correlation turned into a positive one. That's an example of Simpson's paradox: a phenomenon in data visualisation where a trend appears in aggregated groups of data, but disappears or even reverses when grouping information is taken into account. We can make this a bit more clear by using `facets` to separate the three species. In fact, we're making small multiples now! ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = 'black') + facet_grid(~ species) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Remember that the penguins occured on three different islands? Let's facet by `island` as well. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") + facet_grid(island ~ species) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Interesting: apparently the Adelie penguins occur on all three islands, while Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins occur on just one island. We could have found out about this in other ways, ofcourse. Finally; the sex of the penguins was also recorded. We can add that information with color. That will give us a super detailed picture of the penguins dataset, split across three dimensions: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins %>% ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = sex)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + facet_grid(island ~ species) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Apparently for some penguins the sex was not recorded; let's remove them from the dataset before plotting: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- penguins %>% filter(!is.na(sex)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = sex)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + facet_grid(island ~ species) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Good! In fact, there seems to be another Simpson's paradox that's revealed by splitting the dataset by island and sex. Can you find it? Finally, let's change the colors to a color-blind friendly palette and improve the aesthetics. ::: {.column-margin} We're taking the colors from a well-known color-blind friendly palette: [the Okabe-Ito palette](https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.1618). ::: ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} p2 <- p + scale_colour_manual(values = c( "female" = "#E69F00", "male" = "#56B4E9" )) + theme_light() + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") + labs( x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)" ) p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02-data-viz_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: Nice! Finally, let's save the plot. ::: {.cell filename='R'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave('results/small_multiples.png', p2, width = 13, height = 14, units = "cm") ``` ::: Now, save your R script. Then, turn to your terminal in RStudio. We're going to commit these changes to GitHub! ::: {.cell filename='bash'} ```{.bash .cell-code} git status # <1> git add . git status git commit -m "create scatter plot and sina plot" git push ``` ::: 1. `git` sees that you have changed and added files, but it not yet keeping track of them. Alright, we're ready for the assignment now. ## Assignment ::: {.callout-note} ### Assignment You have learned what makes a good visualization. Now do the opposite: make the worst possible figure from the `palmerpenguins` dataset. Aim to commit as many 'data visualisation sins' as you can: - Hide the truth: - Use a barplot with no indication of spread or sample size - Pool across species or sex to hide real patterns - Truncate the y-axis to exaggerate tiny differences - Use unclear visuals: - Use clashing, non-colorblind-friendly colors - Leave axis labels as raw column names, give the plot a misleading title - Map the same variable to color, shape, and size simultaneously - Produce this plot in your R script, save the plot as a `.png` file. - Push all changes to GitHub. - Add you plot into the shared Google Presentations sheet, and add three bullet points describing _why_ your plot is the most ugly and misleading plot ever made. - Also add a link to your GitHub repository in the Google Presentation sheet [here](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1kXmQ_B9e1IF0sSDDtEaR4HYqSqy3RLsXL4BHHgTODlI/edit?usp=sharing){target="_blank"} ::: ## References > [Fundamentals of Data Visualization, Claus O. Wilke](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/)
